pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — 9–11; understand how rainforest products reach everyday life through global SUPPLY CHAINS — palm oil in snacks/soap/cosmetics, soy feeding livestock, cocoa→chocolate, rubber in tyres/gloves, timber→furniture, medicines from forest plants — and that consumer choices can drive either destruction or sustainable practice.
• Standards — UK: DfE KS2 Geography (trade links, economic activity, distribution of natural resources) and Science Y6 (human impact); DT 'where products come from'; leads to KS3.
• Standards — US: NGSS MS-ESS3-4 (human consumption of natural resources) and social-studies global-economics strands.
• Operational details — the core skill is TRACING a chain both ways: forest → plantation/farm → processing → shipping → factory → shelf → your home, AND the reverse (this snack → palm oil → a cleared hillside). Surface the hidden ubiquity of palm oil (in roughly half of packaged supermarket products) as the standout. Then close the FEEDBACK LOOP: because demand pulls the chain, a consumer choosing a certified/sustainable product (or less of it) sends a signal back up the chain — agency, not just guilt. Distinguish 'boycott everything' (can hurt smallholders) from 'choose sustainable', the more nuanced message.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (9): name four rainforest-linked products. Tier B (10): trace how palm oil travels from a forest region to a supermarket shelf. Tier C (11): explain how a specific consumer choice (buying certified) feeds back to reduce deforestation pressure.
bestPractices: Teach tracing BOTH directions: forest→shelf and shelf→forest, so pupils see products as the end of a chain.
Surface palm oil's hidden ubiquity (in ~half of packaged products) as the memorable hook.
Close the feedback loop: demand pulls the chain, so consumer choice can push back — frame as agency, not guilt.
Distinguish 'boycott everything' (can harm smallholders) from 'choose certified/sustainable' as the nuanced message.
Link to prior 'Everyday Foods' and 'Deforestation Drivers' so the chain connects known dots.
keyRepresentations: A supply-chain journey line: forest → farm → processing → shipping → factory → shelf → home.
A 'scan the basket' reveal showing hidden palm oil across everyday products.
Sustainable-vs-unsustainable sourcing toggle with forest-impact and farmer-income meters.
Certification labels (Rainforest Alliance frog, FSC, RSPO) on real packaging.
commonMisconceptions: 'Rainforest products are just exotic foods' — many are hidden ingredients (palm oil in soap, rubber in tyres).
'My shopping can't affect a faraway forest' — consumer demand directly pulls the supply chain.
'Boycotting everything is best' — it can devastate smallholder livelihoods; choosing certified is usually better.
'A product with a green label is automatically fine' — certification helps but varies; it's a signal, not a guarantee.
'Soy is mainly eaten by people as tofu' — most soy feeds livestock worldwide.

learn.summary: Pupils aged 9–11 learn that many everyday products are the far end of global supply chains reaching back into rainforests — palm oil hidden in snacks, soap and cosmetics; soy feeding livestock; cocoa→chocolate; rubber in tyres and gloves; timber→furniture; and medicines from forest plants. The core skill is tracing a chain BOTH directions (forest→plantation→processing→shipping→factory→shelf→home, and the reverse), surfacing palm oil's hidden ubiquity (in roughly half of packaged supermarket products per WWF), and understanding the demand feedback loop: because demand pulls the chain, consumer choices can push back. The nuanced message is 'choose certified/sustainable', not 'boycott everything', because blanket boycotts can harm smallholder farmers and remove incentives to farm sustainably.

activities.title: Build the chain from shelf to forest (and back)
feedback: If a pupil treats a product as unconnected to any forest, prompt: 'Where does the palm oil / rubber / soy in this actually begin? Build the chain one link at a time back to the land.'

If a pupil chooses to boycott everything, point to the collapsed farmer-income meter: 'A total boycott removes smallholders' income and any reward for farming well — what does choosing certified do instead?'

When the basket scan surprises them, reinforce: 'WWF estimates palm oil is in about half of packaged supermarket products — that's why reading labels matters, although in soaps and cosmetics it often appears under other chemical names.'
If a pupil assumes a green label guarantees no harm, note that certification is a signal that helps but varies — it is not an automatic guarantee.
activities.rationale: A supply chain is a trace-and-connect system with a feedback loop. Building the chain in both directions is intended to make products legible as chain endpoints, and a live sourcing toggle with impact/income meters is intended to make the demand→forest→smallholder trade-off more concrete; whether it does so better than simply stating the rule is not established — this is a design proposal, not a validated result. The meters and basket scanner are illustrative interaction examples, not required mechanisms.
sourceClaims: Palm oil is found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products (foods, cosmetics, cleaning products); soy, cocoa, rubber, timber and many medicines are also major rainforest-linked commodities in global supply chains
Consumer demand drives commodity-linked deforestation, and certified sustainable sourcing can reduce pressure while supporting smallholders (boycotts can harm smallholders)
learnerActions: Start from a familiar supermarket product (e.g. a jar of chocolate spread) and build the chain link by link backwards: factory → ship → refinery → plantation → the land, until the last link reaches where the crop was grown, which may be recently cleared forest, at-risk forest or long-established farmland, depending on the source.
Then trace the SAME chain forwards from forest to home, saying each stage aloud or writing it, so the product is seen as the END of a chain, not an isolated thing.

Use a 'scan the basket' reveal: check other everyday items (biscuits, soap, shampoo) and discover how many contain palm oil or palm-derived ingredients. WWF estimates that roughly half of packaged supermarket products do, though the share in any one basket will vary.

For each product, toggle its sourcing from 'cheap/unsustainable' to 'certified' and watch, in this simplified illustrative model, a forest-impact meter fall while a smallholder-income meter holds. Then test boycotting EVERYTHING and see the model's farmer-income meter collapse too. Remember that the model shows a simplified idea, not measured real-world results.
activities.intendedInsight: Everyday shopping is the far end of a chain that reaches into the forest; demand pulls the chain, so the smarter lever is choosing the sustainable link and sending that signal back up the line — not buying nothing.

activities.title: Hidden ingredients hunt
feedback: If a pupil limits the link to obvious tropical foods, read a soap or bread label together and surface the palm oil.
If a pupil thinks soy is mainly eaten by people as tofu, clarify that most soy worldwide feeds livestock, so it is hidden behind meat and eggs.
Praise concrete label-reading evidence rather than guessing: 'You found palm oil listed — that's the kind of clue to look for.'
activities.rationale: Directly addressing the 'just exotic foods' and 'soy is tofu' misconceptions with real labels grounds the ubiquity point in evidence pupils gather themselves. The sort can check classification but does not by itself elicit the label-reading or explanation, so it is paired with gathering real evidence.
sourceClaims: Palm oil is found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products (foods, cosmetics, cleaning products); soy, cocoa, rubber, timber and many medicines are also major rainforest-linked commodities in global supply chains
learnerActions: Read real ingredient labels on everyday packaging together (biscuits, bread, soap, shampoo), and check product descriptions or material labels for items like trainers, which do not carry ingredient lists.

List the non-obvious rainforest-linked ingredients — palm oil or palm derivatives in some soaps and breads, natural rubber in some trainer soles (many use synthetic rubber), and soy animal feed behind much meat and many eggs (not shown on the label).
Sort products into 'obvious tropical treat' (chocolate, bananas, coffee) versus 'hidden ingredient' and discuss why the hidden ones are easy to miss.
Spot certification labels where they appear (Rainforest Alliance frog, FSC, RSPO) and discuss what signal they send.
activities.intendedInsight: Rainforest products are not only exotic jungle foods — many are hidden ingredients in ordinary goods, including palm oil, soy animal feed, rubber and timber.

activities.title: Sequence and match the journey (check and consolidate)
feedback: If sequencing is wrong, ask what has to happen to raw forest produce before it can reach a shelf (it must be grown, processed, shipped, manufactured).
For the certified question, if a pupil picks 'boycott', remind them a boycott removes smallholder income and the incentive to farm sustainably.
activities.rationale: Ordering and matching tasks give a clean recognition check of the chain and links. Recognition-only responses confirm recall but do not by themselves elicit the independent construction or feedback-loop reasoning built in the earlier activities, so use this to consolidate rather than to teach the systems intuition.
sourceClaims: Palm oil is found in roughly half of packaged supermarket products (foods, cosmetics, cleaning products); soy, cocoa, rubber, timber and many medicines are also major rainforest-linked commodities in global supply chains
Consumer demand drives commodity-linked deforestation, and certified sustainable sourcing can reduce pressure while supporting smallholders (boycotts can harm smallholders)
learnerActions: Order the stages of the palm-oil journey in sequence: forest → plantation → processing/refinery → shipping → factory → shelf → home.
Match everyday products to their hidden rainforest ingredient (biscuit→palm oil, tyre→rubber, chicken nugget→soy feed, furniture→timber).
Answer: how does choosing a certified product help a forest compared with buying carelessly OR boycotting everything?
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates the chain order, the product→ingredient links, and the reasoning that certified sourcing is usually better than both careless buying and a blanket boycott.

activities.title: Argue the diagnostic both ways
feedback: If a pupil says distant shopping has no effect, trace one concrete product (palm oil in biscuits, or soy fed to nugget chicken) back to the land where it was grown, which in some supply chains is cleared forest, to show how demand pulls supply.
If a pupil insists boycott is ideal, explain palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop so alternatives can need MORE land, and that certification rewards good practice a boycott cannot.
Reward answers that get BOTH halves and apply them to a fresh product, not slogans like 'rainforest products are bad'.
activities.rationale: The two-tier diagnostic discriminates between a slogan and real reasoning: a pupil must see the connection AND the boycott trade-off. Applying to a new product tests transfer rather than recall.
sourceClaims: Consumer demand drives commodity-linked deforestation, and certified sustainable sourcing can reduce pressure while supporting smallholders (boycotts can harm smallholders)
learnerActions: Respond to a friend's claim: 'My shopping in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing to do is boycott every single rainforest product.'
State clearly whether the friend is right on EACH of the two points, and explain WHY for each half.
Apply the reasoning to a NEW product of the pupil's choice: pick something used this morning and trace an ingredient back toward a rainforest, saying where to look on the label.
Discuss trade-offs: if everyone boycotted palm oil tomorrow, who is helped and who harmed; and is it fair to expect a family on a tight budget to pay more for certified goods?
activities.intendedInsight: Genuine supply-chain reasoning holds both halves: everyday shopping IS connected through demand, AND a blanket boycott is not the best answer because it harms smallholders and removes the reward for farming sustainably.

constraints: Teach tracing in BOTH directions (forest→shelf and shelf→forest) so products are understood as the end of a chain.
Frame consumer choice as agency, not guilt: demand pulls the chain, so choosing sustainably pushes back.
Distinguish 'boycott everything' (can harm smallholders and remove incentive to farm sustainably) from 'choose certified/sustainable' as the more nuanced message.
Present certification labels as a helpful signal that varies, not an automatic guarantee that a product is harmless.
Link to prior work on everyday foods and deforestation drivers so the chain connects known ideas.
Impact and income meters, basket scanners and sourcing toggles are illustrative interaction examples to make the feedback loop concrete; they are optional, not mandatory mechanisms.
Recognition tasks (sequencing, matching, multiple choice) consolidate and check recall but do not on their own elicit the independent construction and trade-off reasoning the objective requires.
Deep stakeholder dialogue (e.g. hearing a smallholder's voice) is a valuable extension but belongs to a later futures/stakeholder node; the focus here is tracing the chain and consumer feedback.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; the three sources were not re-fetched and all carry verified:false in the original row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The 'roughly half of packaged supermarket products contain palm oil' figure is attributed to WWF in the source but was not independently verified here; present it as a sourced estimate, not an exact fact.

The 'palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop / alternatives can need more land' point used in activity 4 feedback comes from the original reteach move and is sourced but unverified; keep it qualified.

The 'most soy worldwide feeds livestock' claim comes from the original misconception list with no attached source; it is widely accepted but was not independently verified here, so keep it as a general statement rather than a cited fact.

The original artefact note 'a 2D interactive is ideal and 3D adds nothing' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; preserved as alternatives with stated affordances/limits rather than universal claims.

The claim that a tap-to-reveal map 'can't let pupils feel the demand→forest feedback that a model makes felt' is a catalog-level comparison, not established comparative efficacy; softened to a scoped affordance note.
The KS2-geography source claim supports topic/curriculum coverage and was removed from activity 1's sourceClaims, where the rationale concerns system design rather than curriculum coverage.

probeDeeper: Pick something you used this morning and try to trace an ingredient back to a rainforest — where would you look on the label?
If everyone suddenly boycotted palm oil tomorrow, who would be helped and who might be harmed, and why?
Why might a 'certified sustainable' label be better for a forest than either buying carelessly OR boycotting completely?
What if a certified product costs more — is it fair to expect a family on a tight budget to pay extra to protect a forest?
assess.correctAnswer: Wrong on both. Ordinary shopping IS linked to rainforests: palm oil is in roughly half of packaged supermarket goods, and soy (mostly for animal feed), cocoa, coffee, natural rubber, beef and timber all come partly from cleared or at-risk forest land — consumer demand pulls the whole supply chain. But boycotting everything is not the best answer either: it can wreck the livelihoods of smallholder farmers and give them no reason to farm sustainably. The stronger choice is to buy certified sustainable products (RSPO palm oil, Rainforest Alliance, FSC), waste less, and push companies to clean up their supply chains.

errorPatterns.pattern: my shopping can't affect a distant forest ('it's on the other side of the world, nothing to do with me')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace one concrete product — palm oil in biscuits, or soy fed to the chicken in a nugget — back to cleared land; show demand pulling supply.
errorPatterns.distractor: Right — shopping in Britain is far too far away to have any effect on a rainforest.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child denies any link between everyday purchases and rainforest clearance, treating the forest as too remote to be touched by demand

errorPatterns.pattern: boycotting every rainforest product is the best thing to do ('just ban palm oil / never buy any of it')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Explain that palm oil is the highest-yielding oil crop — switching to alternatives can need MORE land — and that certified sustainable sourcing rewards good practice; boycott removes that lever.
errorPatterns.distractor: The best thing to do is boycott and never buy any rainforest product at all.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child treats a total boycott as the ideal action and cannot see the harm to smallholders or the loss of any incentive to farm sustainably

errorPatterns.pattern: only exotic 'jungle' foods come from rainforests ('it's just bananas, chocolate and coffee')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read ingredient labels together and list the non-obvious ones (palm oil in soap and bread, rubber in trainers, soy behind meat and eggs).
errorPatterns.distractor: Only obvious tropical treats like chocolate, bananas and coffee are linked to rainforests.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: child limits the link to obviously tropical treats and overlooks hidden ingredients — palm oil, soy animal feed, rubber, timber — in everyday goods

responseLevels.gap: Insists distant shopping has no effect, or parrots 'rainforest products are bad, ban them' — no supply-chain link and no sense of trade-offs.
responseLevels.full: Explains that consumer demand pulls the supply chain so everyday goods (including hidden palm oil and soy feed) are connected, argues that certified sustainable sourcing beats a blanket boycott because a boycott harms smallholders and removes the incentive to do better, and applies this to a new product.
responseLevels.partial: Recognises SOME products come from rainforests and that individual choices matter, but treats boycott as the obvious fix, or names the link without grasping that demand drives clearance across a whole supply chain.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A friend says: 'My shopping at the supermarket in Britain can't possibly affect a rainforest thousands of miles away — and anyway, the best thing anyone can do is boycott every single rainforest product.' Are they right on either point? Tell me WHY.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks distant shopping is disconnected can't see how demand drives clearance. A child who has absorbed 'rainforest products are bad, so ban them all' misses that a blanket boycott harms the very farmers and gives no market reward for doing it right. Getting BOTH halves right — connected AND a boycott is not the answer — shows genuine supply-chain reasoning rather than a slogan.
